n: Ten years have passed, and Sarai still has no children. Her Egyptian servant, Hagar, is introduced—perhaps acquired during their stay in Egypt (12:16).

f.g: A female servant, usually personally attached to her mistress.

n: Sarai proposes a custom known from ancient Near Eastern documents: a childless wife could give her servant to her husband, and the child would count as hers. Abram agrees.

f.w: I may obtain children by her
f.g: Literally “I may be built up by her”—Hebrew banah (build) sounds like ben (son).

f.w: Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai

n: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife. Latter-day revelation teaches that Sarah did this in keeping with God’s law, and that Abraham was not condemned for it.
Hagar becomes pregnant and begins to look down on Sarai. In a culture that prized children, motherhood raised Hagar’s status and hurt Sarai deeply.

f.g: Looked on with contempt; treated as lesser.

n: Sarai blames Abram for the tension and calls on the Lord to judge. Plans made to help often bring unexpected heartache.

f.g: “You are responsible for the wrong done to me.”

n: Abram leaves the matter to Sarai, who treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar runs away. Scripture does not hide the flaws of its heroes.

f.g: Treated her harshly. The same Hebrew word describes Egypt’s oppression of Israel (Exodus 1:11-12).

n: The angel of the Lord finds Hagar by a spring on the road back toward Egypt. God seeks out the outsider, the servant, the runaway.

f.g: A heavenly messenger who speaks with God’s own voice; this is his first appearance in the Bible.
A desert region between Canaan and Egypt.

n: The angel calls Hagar by name and asks where she has come from and where she is going—questions that invite reflection, much like God’s questions in Eden.

f.w: whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?
f.g: “Where have you come from, and where are you going?”

n: The angel tells Hagar to return and submit to Sarai. It is a hard instruction, but it comes with promises of blessing.
Hagar receives a promise much like Abram’s: descendants too many to count. God’s care reaches beyond the covenant line.

f.w: I will multiply thy seed exceedingly

n: Hagar is told to name her son Ishmael, “God hears,” because the Lord has heard her suffering.

f.w: the LORD hath heard thy affliction

n: Ishmael will live free and fierce, like a wild donkey in the desert, never subject to anyone. This describes the independent desert peoples descended from him.

f.g: Literally “a wild donkey of a man”—free-roaming and untamed, not a criticism of his character.

f.w: in the presence of all his brethren
f.g: Or “in defiance of” or “east of” his relatives.

n: Hagar gives God a name: “Thou God seest me.” She is the only person in the Bible to name God. The overlooked servant discovers that God sees her.

f.g: Hebrew El Roi—“the God who sees me.”

n: The spring is named “Well of the Living One who sees me,” a reminder of God’s care in the wilderness.

f.g: “Well of the Living One who sees me.” Isaac later lives near here (24:62; 25:11).

n: Hagar returns and gives birth, and Abram names his son Ishmael—confirming the name given by the angel.
Abram is eighty-six when Ishmael is born. Thirteen more years will pass before God speaks again about the promised son through Sarai.
